Title: TSH-based protocol, tablet instability, and absorption effects on L-T4 bioequivalence
Authors: Eisenberg M, Distefano JJ.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: FDA Guidance for pharmacokinetic (PK) testing of levothyroxine (L-T(4)) for interbrand bioequivalence has evolved recently. Concerns remain about efficacy and safety of the current protocol, based on PK analysis following supraphysiological L-T(4) dosing in euthyroid volunteers, and recent recalls due to intrabrand manufacturing problems also suggest need for further refinement. We examine these interrelated issues quantitatively, using simulated what-if scenarios testing efficacy of a TSH-based protocol and tablet stability and absorption, to enhance precision of L-T(4) bioequivalence methods.
METHODS: We use an updated simulation model of human thyroid hormone regulation quantified and validated from data that span a wide range of normal and abnormal thyroid system function. Bioequivalence: We explored a TSH-based protocol, using normal replacement dosing in simulated thyroidectomized patients, switching brands after 8 weeks of full replacement dosing. We simulated effects of tablet potency differences and intestinal absorption differences on predicted plasma TSH, T(4), and triiodothyronine (T(3)) dynamics. Stability: We simulated effects of potency decay and lot-by-lot differences in realistic scenarios, using actual tablet potency data spanning 2 years, comparing the recently reduced 95-105% FDA-approved potency range with the original 90-110% range.
RESULTS: A simulated decrease as small as 10-15% in L-T(4) or its absorption generated TSH concentrations outside the bioequivalence target range (0.5-2.5 mU/L TSH), whereas T(3) and T(4) plasma levels were maintained normal. For a 25% reduction, steady-state TSH changed 300% (from 1.5 to 6 mU/L) compared with <25% for both T(4) and T(3) (both within their reference ranges). Stability: TSH, T(4), and T(3) remained within normal ranges for most potency decay scenarios, but tablets of the same dose strength and brand were not bioequivalent between lots and between fresh and near-expired tablets.
CONCLUSIONS: A pharmacodynamic TSH-measurement bioequivalence protocol, using normal L-T(4) replacement dosing in athyreotic volunteers, is likely to be more sensitive and safer than current FDA Guidance based on T(4) PK. The tightened 95-105% allowable potency range for L-T(4) tablets is a significant improvement, but otherwise acceptable potency differences (whether due to potency decay or lot-by-lot inconsistencies) may be problematic for some patients, for example, those undergoing high-dose L-T(4) therapy for cancer.

Title: Bioequivalence Study of Two Formulations of Flunarizine Hydrochloride Capsules in Healthy Chinese Subjects Under Fasting and Fed Conditions
Authors: Yang Y, Kai J, Lv D, Zhou H, Yu Y, Shentu J, Wu G.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Flunarizine, a selective calcium channel blocker with vasodilatory and neuroprotective effects, is a mainstay for migraine prophylaxis and vertigo management. This study aimed to compare the bioequivalence, pharmacokinetics, and safety of test and reference flunarizine hydrochloride capsules after a single oral dose under fasting/fed conditions.
METHODS: A randomized, open-label, two-formulation, single-dose, two-period crossover bioequivalence study was conducted under fasting and fed conditions. Eligible healthy Chinese subjects received a single 5-mg dose of the test or reference flunarizine hydrochloride capsules, followed by a 21-day washout interval between periods. Blood samples were collected up to 36 h post-dose. Pharmacokinetic parameters were calculated using noncompartmental methods, and bioequivalence was assessed via geometric mean ratios of the test/reference for primary pharmacokinetic parameters, along with 90% confidence intervals. Tolerability was evaluated during the entire study period.
RESULTS: Twenty-four volunteers completed the fasting study, while 42 volunteers completed the fed study. The test formulation demonstrated bioequivalence to the marketed formulation, with 90% confidence intervals for geometric mean ratios of peak plasma concentration (fasting: 97.38-106.57%; fed: 92.71-109.58%), area under the curve from time 0 to 36 h (fasting: 98.20-108.09%; fed: 93.79-100.81%), and AUC from time 0 to infinity (fasting: 97.88-107.30%; fed: 93.63-100.53%), all within equivalence limits of 80.00-125.00%. High-fat meals delayed the time to maximum concentration by 2.5 h and increased exposure by 20%. Both the test and reference formulations were well tolerated, and no serious adverse events related to the study drug were reported during the study.
CONCLUSIONS: This study confirmed that test and reference flunarizine hydrochloride capsules were bioequivalent under fasting and fed conditions.

Background and Objectives Flunarizine, a selective calcium channel blocker with vasodilatory and neuroprotective effects, is a mainstay for migraine prophylaxis and vertigo management. This study aimed to compare the bioequivalence, pharmacokinetics, and safety of test and reference flunarizine hydrochloride capsules after a single oral dose under fasting/fed conditions. Methods A randomized, open-label, two-formulation, single-dose, two-period crossover bioequivalence study was conducted under fasting and fed conditions. Eligible healthy Chinese subjects received a single 5-mg dose of the test or reference flunarizine hydrochloride capsules, followed by a 21-day washout interval between periods. Blood samples were collected up to 36 h post-dose. Pharmacokinetic parameters were calculated using noncompartmental methods, and bioequivalence was assessed via geometric mean ratios of the test/reference for primary pharmacokinetic parameters, along with 90% confidence intervals. Tolerability was evaluated during the entire study period. Results Twenty-four volunteers completed the fasting study, while 42 volunteers completed the fed study. The test formulation demonstrated bioequivalence to the marketed formulation, with 90% confidence intervals for geometric mean ratios of peak plasma concentration (fasting: 97.38–106.57%; fed: 92.71–109.58%), area under the curve from time 0 to 36 h (fasting: 98.20–108.09%; fed: 93.79–100.81%), and AUC from time 0 to infinity (fasting: 97.88–107.30%; fed: 93.63–100.53%), all within equivalence limits of 80.00–125.00%. High-fat meals delayed the time to maximum concentration by 2.5 h and increased exposure by 20%. Both the test and reference formulations were well tolerated, and no serious adverse events related to the study drug were reported during the study. Conclusions This study confirmed that test and reference flunarizine hydrochloride capsules were bioequivalent under fasting and fed conditions. Introduction Migraine is a neurological disorder characterized by intense debilitating headaches that may last for several hours or even days. It is often accompanied by additional symptoms, such as nausea and vomiting [ 1 ]. The 1-year prevalence of migraines is estimated at approximately 15% [ 2 , 3 ], with the condition potentially developing at any age, including in infants [ 4 ]. According to the World Health Organization, migraine is ranked as the sixth most disabling condition globally and the most disabling among neurological disorders [ 5 ]. Consequently, migraines impose a significant burden on individuals’ daily quality of life, highlighting the need for effective and timely treatment. Flunarizine, introduced in the 1980s, is commonly used in the management of migraine [ 6 ]. As a non-selective calcium channel blocker, it also antagonizes dopamine D 2 receptors and exhibits antihistamine effects [ 7 , 8 ]. Flunarizine, a medication that works by inhibiting vascular smooth muscle contraction and modulating neuronal excitability, has been shown to reduce both the frequency and intensity of migraine attacks [ 9 ]. Flunarizine is commonly prescribed in various regions, including Europe, Japan, and China, for migraine prevention in adults, while its use in pediatric populations is more restricted [ 10 – 15 ]. Numerous national treatment guidelines recommend flunarizine as a first-line prophylactic option for migraine management, supported by level A evidence, with a typical dose range of 5–10 mg [ 12 , 16 ]. However, common side effects include weight gain, fatigue, mood changes, and drowsiness [ 12 , 15 ]. To minimize the impact of daytime drowsiness, it is generally recommended that flunarizine be taken at bedtime. Following oral administration, flunarizine is well absorbed, with peak plasma concentrations occurring 2–4 h post-dose [ 17 ]. With consistent daily dosing of 10 mg, plasma concentrations gradually increase, reaching steady-state concentrations after approximately 5–6 weeks of treatment. The large apparent volume of distribution (range = 26.7–79.9 L/kg) observed after oral administration suggests extensive tissue distribution of flunarizine [ 17 ]. The elimination half-life ( t 1/2 ) of flunarizine after long-term use ranges from 4 to 19 days [ 17 ]. It is primarily metabolized in the liver via N-oxidation and aromatic hydroxylation [ 18 ]. Follow a single dose, less than 7% of flunarizine and its metabolites were recovered in feces and urine within 48 h [ 17 ]. The aim was to evaluate the pharmacokinetics, bioequivalence (BE), and safety of two formulations of flunarizine. The test formulation was developed by Chiatai Qingchunbao Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd., China, while the reference formulation, Sibelium ® , was produced by Xi’an Janssen Pharmaceutica Ltd., China. The evaluation was conducted following a single-dose administration of both formulations. This study also aims to provide evidence supporting the approval of generic flunarizine formulations in China. Materials and Methods Ethics Statement of Human Rights With the registration number ChiCTR1900026713, this study was recorded with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry. Approval No. 2018-EC-333 was given after the study protocol and informed consent forms were reviewed and approved by the independent Ethics Committee at the First Affiliated Hospital, School of Medicine, Zhejiang University. The phase I clinical trial unit of The First Affiliated Hospital was the sole site of the clinical procedures. Good Clinical Practice guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki were followed throughout the research. Before taking part in any study procedures, all participants were asked to provide written informed permission. Study Participants Healthy volunteers had to be between the ages of 18 and 45 years and have a body mass index between 19 and 26 kg/m 2 . Male participants were required to be at least 50 kg in weight, while female participants were required to be at least 45 kg. In order to be eligible to participate, individuals had to have a clean bill of health according to the study’s inclusion criteria, which included no major health issues as shown by their medical records, electrocardiograms, clinical laboratory tests, vital signs, or physical exams. In addition, the kidney and liver function laboratory values at baseline were required to be within normal limits. All female participants were required to utilize effective methods of birth control during the study and for a minimum of 6 months after the last dose, and they must not be pregnant when they enrolled. The study did not include any participants who fulfilled any of the exclusion criteria listed in the protocol. Subjects who had anaphylactic reactions to any aspect of the experimental product or had a history of clinical medication allergies were also not allowed to participate. Additionally, subjects could not participate if they tested positive for human immunodeficiency virus or hepatitis B or C. Additional exclusion criteria were being a smoker or user of nicotine products within 3 months before the study, taking any vitamins, herbs, or medications within 2 weeks before the study drug was given, and taking any medications that alter cytochrome P450 enzymes within 30 days before enrolling. Subjects who drank alcohol or ate foods high in caffeine within 2 days of the trial also were not allowed to participate. Study Drugs The 5-mg capsules with an active ingredient content of 96.2% were supplied by Chiatai Qingchunbao Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. of Hangzhou, China. The batch number is 1903301, and the expiration date is 11 March, 2023. Sibelium ® , a 5-mg capsule with the batch number 180902850 serving as the reference formulation, was manufactured in China by Xi’an Janssen Pharmaceutical Ltd. Study Design There were two separate parts to this research: the fasting condition and the fed condition. Both studies used a two-sequence, two-period, randomized, open-label, two-formulation, crossover BE design. Researchers used a random number table developed by SAS statistical software (version 9.4) to assign participants to one of two treatment sequences: test-reference or reference-test, with a 1:1 allocation ratio. Each subject took a single oral dose of a flunarizine hydrochloride 5-mg capsule as a test or reference formulation during each treatment period. Between each treatment phase, a washout period of 21 days (± 2 days) was put in place to make sure that the previous dose was cleared out. Two days before each treatment phase, subjects were hospitalized to the phase I clinical trial unit to standardize their nutritional consumption and physical activity levels. After an overnight fast of at least 10 h, participants in the fasting condition took one 5-mg oral dose of the test or reference formulation with 240 mL of warm water. Thirty minutes before medication delivery, individuals in the fed group ate a standardized high-fat meal (800–1000 kcal), with about 150 kcal coming from protein, 250 kcal from carbohydrates, and 500–600 kcal from fat. Water intake was not permitted from 1 h prior to dosing until 1 h post-dosing, except for 240 mL of water allowed for swallowing the drug. At 4 and 10 h after the medication was administered, standardized meals were given. Sample Size Based on clinical pharmacology and biopharmaceutical reviews, flunarizine is not classified as a highly variable drug. Consequently,, the coefficient of intra-individual variation (CV intra ) for the maximum plasma concentration ( C max ) and the area under the curve (AUC) is presumed to be less than 30%. For the fasting condition, the CV intra for C max and AUC was assumed to be 20%. With a one-sided α of 0.05 and a power of 0.8 ( β = 0.2), the geometric mean ratio (GMR) between the test and reference formulations was expected to fall between 0.95 and 1.05, with a 90% confidence interval (CI) of 80.00–125.00. Thus, the fasting study required 20 participants. After accounting for potential dropouts, 24 subjects were enrolled for the fasting condition. Given that postprandial conditions could delay the time to C max and affect bioavailability, the CV intra for C max and AUC under the fed condition was estimated at 29%, with the remaining assumptions unchanged. Therefore, 36 participants were required for the fed condition, and 42 participants were ultimately enrolled after considering the dropout rate. Biological Sample Collection Previous studies indicate that flunarizine reaches its C max of approximately 20 ng/mL within 1–3 h [ 18 – 20 ]. The terminal t 1/2 is significantly influenced by the duration of sampling: a 24-h sampling window yields a t 1/2 of 5–7 h, while a 72-h window reveals approximately 31 h [ 18 – 20 ]. By 24 h, mean concentrations decline to ≤ 2 ng/mL, which is less than 10% of C max . For immediate-release BE studies, guidelines stipulate that the sampling schedule must include frequent sampling around the predicted time to C max ( T max ) to provide a reliable estimate of peak exposure. Additionally, the plasma concentration–time curve should be sufficiently extended to ensure that the AUC from time zero to time t (AUC 0– t ) encompasses at least 80% of the AUC from time zero to infinity (AUC 0–∞ ). Based on these findings, we have designed a 36-h sample schedule. Within the fasting condition, blood samples were collected at pre-dose (0.0 h) and at 0.5, 1.0, and 1.33 h (1 h 20 min), 1.67 h (1 h 40 min), 2.0 and 2.33 h (2 h 20 min), 2.67 h (2 h 40 min), 3.0 and 3.33 h (3 h 20 min), 3.67 h (3 h 40 min), and 4.0, 4.5, 5.0, 5.5, 6.0, 8.0, 10.0, 12.0, 24.0, and 36.0 h after dosing. When comparing the fed and fasting settings, the difference in T max was about 3.5 h. Here, blood samples were taken at pre-dose (0.0 h) and at 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, and 3.33 h (3 h 20 min), 3.67 h (3 h 40 min), 4.0 and 4.33 h (4 h 20 min), 4.67 h (4 h 40 min), 5.0 and 5.33 h (5 h 20 min), 5.67 h (5 h 40 min), and 6.0, 8.0, 10.0, 12.0, 24.0, and 36.0 h after dosing. The blood samples were centrifuged at 2000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C, and the plasma was stored at − 60 °C until analysis. Plasma Drug Concentration Analysis Plasma concentrations of flunarizine were determined at Nanjing Kelitai Pharmaceutical Technology Co., Ltd. (Nanjing, China) using a validated, sensitive, and specific high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry method. The system comprised an LC-20AD™ (Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan) coupled with an API 4000 mass spectrometer (AB SCIEX, Framingham, MA, USA). Chromatography was performed using a Kinetex 2.6 μm XB-C18 column (50 × 2.1 mm) equipped with a Phenomenex Security Guard Cartridges C18 (4 × 2.0 mm). The mobile phase consisted of 0.5% formic acid and 10.0 mM of NH4Ac in water (mobile phase A) and acetonitrile (mobile phase B) running at a flow rate of 0.4 mL/min. The gradient elution program was as follows: 0–1.7 min, 52%A/48%B; 1.8–2.5 min, 0%A/100%B; 2.6–4.0 min, 52%A/48%B. Quantification was performed using multiple reaction monitoring of the transitions m / z 405.2 → 203.2 for flunarizine and m / z 413.2→203.2 for flunarizine-d8 (internal standard). The assay exhibited linearity within the concentration range of 0.250–60.0 ng/mL, with a lower limit of quantitation (LLOQ) of 0.250 ng/mL. In the blank matrix, we did not observe any interference at the peak location of flunarizine and internal standard, which indicates that the liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry analysis method was highly selective. No carry-over effect was observed, as the injection of wash following plasma with the highest spiked concentration showed no detectable peaks (< 20 % of the LLOQ) at the retention times of flunarizine or the internal standard. In plasma samples, the intra- and inter-day precision (coefficient of variation) for the LLOQ was below 7.1%. Furthermore, the intra- and inter-day accuracy for LLOQ ranged from 90.8 to 99.2%. The intra- and inter-day precision for nominal concentrations of low (LQC, 0.700 ng/mL), low-medium (MQC1, 8.00 ng/mL), medium (MQC2, 18.0 ng/mL), and high (HQC, 45.0 ng/mL) quality-control samples was below 3.7%. The intra-day accuracy ranged from 95.1 to 102.4%, while the inter-day accuracy ranged from 96.7 to 100.9%. Stability tests indicated that plasma sample decomposition was less than 10% for all conditions examined (19 h at room temperature, five freeze-thaw cycles at − 70 °C, and 107 days of storage at or below −70 °C). Safety Assessments A variety of safety parameters were monitored, including electrocardiograms, vital signs, clinical laboratory tests, and adverse events (AEs). The AEs were classified and graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events , version 4.3. The Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities was used for recording these events, with system organ class and preferred term serving as the determining factors. Research physicians and volunteers both reported AEs throughout the trial. Follow-up for participants experiencing AEs continued until their symptoms or corresponding physical and clinical examination results returned to normal or baseline levels, or until the participant chose not to attend further follow-up visits. Pharmacokinetic and Statistical Analyses The flunarizine pharmacokinetic (PK) parameters were determined using a non-compartmental model in Phoenix WinNonlin software (version 7.0). The C max and T max were taken directly from the plasma concentration–time profiles. The AUC from 0 to 36 h (AUC 0–36h ) was computed using the trapezoidal rule. The AUC 0–∞ was calculated by adding the AUC 0–36h and the ratio of the last measurable concentration to the elimination rate constant. The elimination rate constant was found by running a log-linear regression analysis on the plasma concentration data during the terminal elimination phase. The elimination t 1/2 was then calculated as 0.693/elimination rate constant. The effects of formulation, treatment period, dosing sequence, and individual individuals were assessed by analysis of variance using a linear mixed model, after C max , AUC 0–36h , and AUC 0–∞ were transformed to their natural logarithmic values. The GMR and associated 90% CI for the test-to-reference formulation were determined using the logarithmically converted major PK parameters. If the 90% CIs for the GMR of the main PK parameters were between 80.00 and 125.00%, it was determined that BE had occurred. The T max was compared between the two versions using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results Subject Characteristics The study was conducted from 14 October, 2019 to 19 December, 2019. included all subjects who received at least one dose of the study drug. In the fasting study, 24 participants were part of the SS. A total of 11 AEs were reported across 11 subjects, yielding an incidence rate of 45.8% (11/24). Six AEs occurred in six participants receiving the reference product, with an incidence of 6.67% (6/24), while five AEs were reported by five participants in the test product group, corresponding to an incidence rate of 5.63% (5/24). All AEs were classified as grade 1 and resolved spontaneously without specific treatment. Notably, one participant exhibited elevated serum triglyceride levels that did not return to baseline during the follow-up period. In the fed study, 42 participants were included in the SS. A total of 27 AEs were reported by 16 subjects, resulting in an incidence rate of 38.1% (16/42). The AE incidence was 33.3% (8/42) in the test product group and 41.7% (10/42) in the reference product group. Similar to the fasting study, all AEs were of grade 1 severity and resolved spontaneously without the need for specific intervention. These findings suggest that both the test and reference formulations of flunarizine were well tolerated and safe in healthy volunteers, irrespective of the fasting or fed conditions. Additionally, the study provided valuable insights into the pharmacokinetics of flunarizine within this cohort. Both formulations were well tolerated, with no severe AEs associated with the study drug. For most BE studies, a sample size of 18–24 subjects is typically sufficient. In this trial, the CV intra for C max and AUC under fasting conditions was 9.12% and 9.71%, respectively. Under fed conditions, the CV intra for C max was 23.05%, while AUC had a CV intra of 9.84%. These CV intra values for C max were slightly lower than those reported in a previous study, where the values were 14.78% for the fasting condition and 23.65% for the fed condition [ 20 ]. In both conditions, the CV intra for all parameters was less than 30%, indicating that the sample size and study design were robust enough to ensure sufficient statistical power for meeting BE criteria. The study’s 21-day washout period was carefully designed based on the PK profile of flunarizine. Because of its high lipophilicity, flunarizine tends to accumulate in tissues and exhibits prolonged redistribution, which can result in detectable plasma concentrations (> 0.5 ng/mL) even 30 days after administration in a small subset of individuals. To minimize the potential for interference from residual drug concentrations and address inter-individual variability, the washout period was extended to 21 days, exceeding the typical 5 × terminal t 1/2 recommendation. After this washout period, residual flunarizine concentrations in 13 subjects (median 0.292 ng/mL, range 0.255–0.426 ng/mL) were confirmed to be well below 5% of the C max for each subject during that period. This strategy helped maintain the stability of key physiological markers, ensured operational efficiency with a total study duration of fewer than 28 days, and maximized the inclusion of evaluable PK data for the BE analysis. When comparing the PK parameters of flunarizine with those reported in previous studies [ 17 – 21 ], the observed values for C max and T max were consistent with those documented in the Chinese population, thus supporting the validity of our results. However, the C max in this study was lower than that reported in healthy Indian volunteers (17.34 vs 32.14 ng/mL) [ 22 ]. This discrepancy may be attributed to ethnic differences or genetic polymorphisms. The elimination t 1/2 of the reference flunarizine formulation was 8.98 ± 1.50 h under fasting conditions and 9.37 ± 2.55 h following food intake. These values are within the range specified for the labeled reference product (5–15 h) but are shorter than those observed in studies with extended sampling durations [ 21 , 22 ]. This difference can be explained by the variations in the timing of terminal phase sampling. In our BE study, the elimination t 1/2 was estimated using a 36-h post-dose sampling window. Despite the relatively shorter duration, the mean plasma concentration of flunarizine at 36 h post-dose was as low as 1.2 ng/mL, which is well below one tenth of the observed C max . This indicates that our sampling schedule sufficiently captured the plasma concentration–time profile, providing a reliable measure of drug exposure and enabling an accurate estimation of AUC 0–∞ . Our study design resulted in an average AUC 0–36h /AUC 0–∞ ratio of 92.33% under both fasting and fed conditions. Each individual AUC 0–36h /AUC 0–∞ value is more than 83.96%, surpassing the recommended threshold of 80% [ 23 , 24 ]. Based on these findings, a sampling period longer than 36 h is not considered necessary for BE studies of immediate-release flunarizine formulations. Further comparison of the PK data under fasting and fed conditions revealed that food influenced the absorption rate of flunarizine. Specifically, the mean C max increased by 37.4%, and the median T max was delayed from 2.33 h under fasting conditions to 4.67 h after food intake. As a result, the AUC values for flunarizine were significantly higher when administered with food compared with the fasting state. These findings are consistent with previous reports [ 20 , 21 ]. Our study presents a significant advantage concerning the sex composition of volunteers. Given that women experience a three-fold higher prevalence of migraine compared with men [ 25 ], prior BE research has predominantly focused on male participants (78.4–100%), with limited inclusion of female subjects [ 18 – 21 ]. Our study included 26 female volunteers, constituting 42.4% of the total sample. This substantial female representation enabled a robust comparison of PK exposure between sexes. Our analysis revealed no significant differences in the key PK parameters between male and female participants following the single-dose administration of flunarizine (Table 5 ). However, as the majority of participants were aged between 18 and 40 years, further research is warranted to explore the pharmacokinetics of flunarizine in older populations. Given that flunarizine is primarily metabolized in the liver, caution is advised when using the drug in patients with severe liver dysfunction. Additionally, as the drug may accumulate with repeated use, further studies are needed to assess its safety and efficacy in individuals with liver impairment. All reported AEs were mild to moderate in nature, with no serious AEs documented. Overall, both the test and reference formulations demonstrated good tolerance among all participants. Conclusions The findings of this inquiry demonstrate that the generic flunarizine hydrochloride capsules available in China exhibit BE to the reference formulation (Sibelium ® ) regarding both the rate and extent of absorption, observed under fasting and fed states. Both formulations exhibited a favorable tolerance profile among the healthy Chinese population and can be regarded as interchangeable for clinical applications, potentially contributing to the reduction in the economic burden faced by patients with migraine in China. Title: Pharmacokinetics and Safety Evaluation of a New Generic Sitafloxacin: A Phase I Bioequivalence Study in Healthy Chinese Participants
Authors: Lei Y, Luo P, Chen Y, Xue L, Zhang D, Qi X, Fang Y, Yu H, He Z, Zuo Q, Liu C, Liu D, Ren X, Chen Q.
Citation: Clin Pharmacol Drug Dev. 2025 Aug;14(8):592-597. doi: 10.1002/cpdd.1519. Epub 2025 May 14.
Abstract: Sitafloxacin is a new antibiotic drug belonging to the fourth generation quinolone antibiotics. The aim of this study was to evaluate the pharmacokinetics (PK), safety profiles, and bioequivalence of test and reference 50-mg sitafloxacin tablets under fasting and fed conditions. The PK parameters, which were calculated with noncompartmental model, including maximum concentration, area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) from time 0 to the last quantifiable concentration, and AUC from time 0 to infinity. The bioequivalence was assessed on the basis of whether the 90% confidence intervals of the geometric mean ratio for the test/reference drugs fell within the accepted range of 80%-125%. Adverse events were monitored to assess safety. Finally, 80 healthy Chinese participants were enrolled, of which 40 were enrolled in the fasting study and the other 40 enrolled in the fed study. There was 1 participant in the fed trial who withdrew from the study because of failure to finish the high-fat meal. The geometric mean ratio and its 90% confidence interval for the maximum concentration, AUC from time 0 to the last quantifiable concentration, AUC from time 0 to infinity between the branded and generic sitafloxacin, under both fasting and fed conditions, were compliant with the predefined bioequivalence criteria of 80%-125%. No serious adverse events were observed in this study. Therefore, the findings indicate that generic and original sitafloxacin tablets have comparable bioequivalence and safety profiles.

The development of new antimicrobial drugs is critical to address this growing issue and protect public health. Sitafloxacin is a fourth‐generation fluoroquinolone antibiotic. It shows strong activity against various gram‐positive and ‐negative bacteria, and this new antibiotic offers significant advantages in combating bacterial resistance. 2 , 3 , 4 The oral absorption of sitafloxacin is rapid and complete, with an absolute bioavailability as high as 89%. 5 Additionally, sitafloxacin exhibits approximately 50% serum protein binding and has a short t 1/2 (about 5 hours), and its area under the concentration‐time curve (AUC) increases in proportion to the dose. Moreover, sitafloxacin is primarily eliminated by the kidneys through urine as a prototype. 6 Its main metabolic pathway involves glucuronide conjugation, and it can moderately inhibit the cytochrome P450 1A enzyme without affecting other cytochrome 450 enzymes. Like other fluoroquinolones, sitafloxacin can also interact with metal ion‐containing drugs. 7 Genetic variations in ABCB1 (rs1045642), UGT1A1 (rs2741049), and UGT1A9 (rs3832043) are suspected to impact the maximum concentration (C max ) or t 1/2 of sitafloxacin. 8 Even though branded sitafloxacin has been in use in China for years, a considerable proportion of patients cannot afford it. Therefore, a more affordable generic equivalent is needed to satisfy actual clinical demand. Here, to evaluate the bioequivalence and safety of branded and generic sitafloxacin under both fasting and postprandial states, a Phase I clinical trial was conducted in healthy Chinese participants. Materials and Methods Formulations The test drug of sitafloxacin (batch number: 19090641) was produced by Yangtze River Pharmaceutical Group Co., Ltd. (Jiangsu, China). The reference drug of sitafloxacin (GRACEVIT) (Batch Number: ZAB0146) was produced by Daiichi Sankyo Company Limited (Tokyo, Japan). Participants Eligible participants must fulfill the following criteria for inclusion: (1) comprehension and willingness to sign the informed consent document; (2) male and female participants aged 18‐65 years, weighing 50.0 kg or more for men and 45.0 kg or more for women, with a body mass index within the range of 19.0‐26.0 kg/m 2 ; and (3) participants in good health. Participants were not included if they had any of the following conditions: (1) clinically significant abnormalities in examinations or tests; (2) history of serious diseases in any system; (3) any situation that the investigator considers inappropriate; (4) recent participation in other clinical trials or use of investigational drugs; (5) use of prescription or over‐the‐counter drugs, supplements, vitamins, or Chinese medicine in the past 30 days; (6) pregnant or breastfeeding women; and (7) acute diseases from screening to pre‐administration. Ethics This bioequivalence study (BES) is registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ( http://www.chictr.org.cn/ ; CTR2400091798) and was approved by the Clinical Trial Ethics Committee of Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Ethical Review Document No. 89 [2019]). All participants signed written informed consent forms before taking part in the study. Study Design This study was a randomized, open‐label, 2‐period, 2‐sequence crossover design, assessing bioequivalence in healthy Chinese participants under both fasting and fed states. In the study, qualified participants were randomly allocated to either of the 2 treatment sequences (test‐reference group or reference‐test group) in a 1:1 ratio. They received the study drug once per treatment period, separated by a 7‐day washout period. In the fasting study, qualified participants received a single 50‐mg oral dose of test or reference tablets after fasting overnight, with 240 mL of water. In the fed study, the procedure was similar to the fasting state, except that participants consumed a high‐fat breakfast (800‐1000 kcal) 30 minutes before drug administration. Blood Sampling and Bioanalytical Methods In the fasting study, the blood samples (4 mL per sample) were collected 1 hour before dosing and 0.17, 0.33, 0.5, 0.67, 0.83, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, and 36 hours after dosing, which were placed in an ice bath anticoagulation tube with dipotassium ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid. In the fed study, the blood collection time points varied as 0, 0.17, 0.33, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, and 36 hours, with other inspection items as in the fasting study. The blood samples were centrifuged at 2000 g for 10 minutes (at a temperature of 4°C) to obtain plasma, which was then divided into 2 parts (test sample and backup sample). All samples were stored at −70±10°C within 4 hours after blood collection. The detection method of sitafloxacin was validated by Nanjing KeliTai Pharmaceutical Technology Co., Ltd., using a validated high‐performance liquid chromatography‐tandem mass spectrometry method with sitafloxacin‐d4 as an internal standard. The system includes a Shimadzu liquid chromatography pump, Ultimate XB‐C18 (3 µm, 2.1 × 50 mm; Welch) column, and Triple Quad 6500+ mass spectrometer (Applied Biosystems/Sciex). The column temperature of the chromatography column was 40°C. The mobile phase A was water with 10.0 mmol/L NH 4 Ac and 0.1% formic acid, and the mobile phase B was methanol with 0.1% formic acid. The flow rate was run at 0.5 mL/min. Detection was in multiple reaction monitoring mode with positive ion electrospray ionization. The transition ion pair of 410.1/392.2 was selected for sitafloxacin, as well as the 416.2/398.2 was selected for sitafloxacin‐d4. The method was selective, with no plasma interference. Data acquisition was performed with Analyst software version 1.6.3 (Applied Biosystems/Sciex). After that, the sample pretreatment method is protein precipitation and the extraction efficiencies of both sitafloxacin and the internal standard were between 87.1% and 95.4%. The intra‐assay precision was from 2.9% to 3.7%, and the interassay precision was from 3.4% to 5.6%. Sitafloxacin's standard curve was linear from 2.0 to 1000 ng/mL, with a quantification limit of 2.0 ng/mL. Safety Assessments Participant safety after sitafloxacin tablet administration was assessed through monitoring of clinical observation, laboratory investigation, 12‐lead electrocardiograms, and evaluation of adverse events (AEs) and their frequency. AEs were categorized using the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities Version 23.0, with the analysis primarily using descriptive statistical techniques. The occurrence of AEs and adverse drug reactions was aggregated by the system organ class and the preferred term, detailing both the frequency of cases and the frequency of events. Pharmacokinetics and Statistical Analysis The pharmacokinetic (PK) parameters were derived using the Phoenix WinNonlin Version 8.1 software (Certara). For other statistical analyses, SAS Version 9.4 software (SAS Institute) was used. The PK parameters were calculated with the noncompartmental model, comprising the maximum concentration (C max ), the area under the curve (AUC) from time 0 to the last quantifiable concentration (AUC 0‐t ), and the AUC from time 0 to infinity (AUC 0‐∞ ). The bioequivalence of test and reference sitafloxacin was assessed on the basis of whether the 90% confidence intervals of the geometric mean ratio for AUC 0‐t , AUC 0‐∞ , and C max fell within the accepted range of 80%‐125%. Results General Characteristics of the Participants In the fasted trial, 150 healthy Chinese participants were screened between November 19, 2019, and November 24, 2019. Forty participants were enrolled, and 37 completed 2 cycles with protocol adherence. In the fed trial, 167 healthy Chinese participants were screened between December 27, 2019, and January 1, 2020. Forty participants were enrolled, and 36 participants completed 2 cycles with protocol adherence. The detailed general characteristics of enrolled participants are shown in Table 1S . Pharmacokinetic Parameters In the fasting trial, 2 participants voluntarily withdrew from the study before the administration of medication in the second cycle, and only the PK data from the first cycle were included in the PK analyses and BES. One participant was lost to follow‐up during the AE follow‐up phase, but both cycles of PK blood samples were collected completely according to the protocol, so the PK data were included in both PK analyses and BES. In the fed trial, 4 participants did not complete the trial. One participant withdrew from the trial before the second cycle of medication, and thus only the first cycle of PK data was included in PK analyses and BES. One participant voluntarily withdrew from the study after the 24‐hour blood sample collection following the first cycle of medication. Although the 36‐hour blood sample was missing, the first cycle of PK data was included in PK analyses and BES. Another participant was lost to follow‐up during the AE phase after completing 2 cycles of medication and blood collection, so the PK data were included in both PK analyses and BES. Still, 1 participant did not receive medication and only had a premedication blood sample taken at 0 hour, and was not included in any analysis set. The mean plasma concentration‐time profiles of sitafloxacin under fasting and feeding experiments are shown in Figures 1 and 2 , respectively. John Wiley & Sons, Ltd. Safety The AEs that were observed in this study are detailed in Table 2S . A total of 25 AEs were recorded in 16 participants (40%) in the fasting study; among them, 1 participant experienced 1 episode of blood pressure decrease after taking the reference product, and the potential relationship with the study drug was judged as possibly unrelated. The potential relationship of all other treatment‐emergent AEs was judged as possibly related to the study drug. In addition, a total of 22 AEs were recorded in 16 participants (41%) in the fed study; among them, 1 participant experienced 1 episode of bradycardia (slowing of pulse) before taking the reference product, and the potential association with the study drug was assessed as possibly unrelated. The potential association of all other treatment‐emergent AEs with the study drug was assessed as possibly related. Throughout this study, all AEs were of Grade I. By the end of the trial, all AEs for the participants had been followed up to resolution or recovery, except for the participants who were lost to follow‐up and did not have an outcome documented. No serious AEs or AEs led to the withdrawal of participants. Discussion The present study aims to evaluate the PK, bioequivalence, and safety characteristics of a single oral administration of 50‐mg sitafloxacin tablets of the test and reference preparations in healthy participants under fasting or fed conditions. There were no significant differences in the demographic characteristics of participants between the groups (test and reference). The analysis of PK parameters shows that the PK characteristics of the test and reference preparations are similar. The PK parameters of this study are basically consistent with the data in the literature. 9 That is, a single‐dose PK and safety study in humans that included 12 healthy Chinese volunteers who were randomly assigned to 3 dose groups of 50, 100, and 200 mg (all under fasting conditions). Time to C max was approximately between 0.85 and 1.21 hours, and the t 1/2 was approximately between 5.19 and 6.28 hours. However, our study demonstrated that food decreased the AUC 0‐t , AUC 0‐∞ , and C max of sitafloxacin. These findings are inconsistent with the previous research, which identified that the sitafloxacin exposure was comparable in the fed and fasting states. 6 Notably, there was also a research demonstrated that a high‐fat diet can cause a significantly decreased C max , although no significant changes in the AUC were observed. 8 Actually, sitafloxacin would be vulnerable to interaction with metal ions, indicating there was a logical explanation for the food‐drug interaction observed in our study. Therefore, it is better to administer oral sitafloxacin under fasting. T max of sitafloxacin was prolonged when taken with food in our result which was likely caused by a delay in gastric emptying. This finding is consistent with the observation from previous studies. 6 , 8 The results demonstrated that the GM ratio 90% confidence interval of C max , AUC 0‐t , and AUC 0‐∞ were all in the range of 80%‐125%, in both fasting and fed conditions, suggesting that the 2 formulations are bioequivalent. In the study, all AEs were mild (Grade I), and both drug formulations were well tolerated without SAEs. In the fasting trial, the main AEs were hypotension (20%), supraventricular arrhythmia (7.5%), proteinuria (5%), and right bundle branch block (5%). In the fed trial, hypotension (15.4%) and proteinuria (5.1%) were most common, with other AEs reported only once. Based on postmarketing experience, the common AEs of sitafloxacin include diarrhea, loose stools, elevated alanine transaminase, elevated aspartate transaminase, rash, headache, dizziness, positive urinary protein, and so on. In this trial, no participants reported AEs such as diarrhea or loose stools. However, the adverse reactions judged in this trial, such as blood pressure reduction, supraventricular arrhythmia, and right bundle branch block, have not been previously reported, which is inconsistent with postmarketing experience. Since these reactions all occurred after administration, they were considered possibly related. Nevertheless, all the AEs we recorded were mild, so both formulations were well‐tolerated in our study. Title: Bioequivalence Study of Amitriptyline Hydrochloride Tablets in Healthy Chinese Volunteers Under Fasting and Fed Conditions
Authors: Zhai Y, Wu L, Zheng Y, Wu M, Huang Y, Huang Q, Shentu J, Zhao Q, Liu J.
Citation: Drug Des Devel Ther. 2020 Aug 4;14:3131-3142. doi: 10.2147/DDDT.S258173. eCollection 2020.
Abstract:
PURPOSE: This study compares the pharmacokinetic and safety profiles between a new generic and a branded reference formulation of amitriptyline hydrochloride tablets, and assesses the bioequivalence of the two products in healthy Chinese volunteers to obtain sufficient evidence for the marketing approval of the generic drug.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A randomized, open-label, two-period crossover study (clinicaltrials.gov, NCT03646526) was conducted under both fasting and fed conditions in healthy Chinese volunteers (24 subjects/condition). Eligible subjects randomly received a single 25 mg dose of either the test or the reference formulation, followed by a 3-week washout period. Blood samples were collected until 144 h following administration. The pharmacokinetic parameters were acquired based on the concentration-time profiles, including the areas under the plasma concentration-time curve (AUC<sub>0-t</sub>, AUC<sub>0-∞</sub>), the peak plasma concentration (C<sub>max</sub>), the time to achieve C<sub>max</sub> (T<sub>max</sub>), and the elimination half-life (t<sub>1/2</sub>). The geometric mean ratios (GMRs) and the corresponding 90% confidence intervals (CIs) of amitriptyline were acquired for bioequivalence analysis, and values of these parameters for nortriptyline were used for comparison of therapeutic outcomes. Safety assessments included laboratory tests, physical examination, vital signs, and incidence of adverse events (AEs).
RESULTS: The values of t<sub>1/2</sub> and T<sub>max</sub> for amitriptyline were not significantly different between the test and reference products under both fasting and fed conditions (P > 0.05). The GMRs of C<sub>max</sub>, AUC<sub>0-t</sub>, and AUC<sub>0-∞</sub> between the two products, and corresponding 90% CIs, were all within the range of 80% to 125% under both fasting and fed conditions. The test and reference products were well tolerated and did not elicit serious adverse events.
CONCLUSION: This study demonstrated that the generic and reference products were well tolerated by the subjects and bioequivalent, according to the rate and extent of the drug absorption.

(Hunan, China), the manufacturer of amitriptyline hydrochloride tablets and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 81801644 and No. 81702862). pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement no pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY-NC Introduction Depression is a major mental health disorders, which affected more than 300 million people in 2015. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that depression is the leading cause of disability and results in high morbidity, high suicide rates, and low clinical treatment rates worldwide. 1 Various antidepressants, which are now available, are effective in treating depression, including tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), monoamine oxidase inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors, selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors, and noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressants. 2 , 3 Antidepressants were the 3rd most frequently prescribed drugs to individuals in the United States between 2005 and 2008. 4 , 5 In addition, TCA amitriptyline has been regarded as one of the reference compounds for depression treatment. 6 Amitriptyline, the most commonly used TCA, has a strong sedative effect and is primarily used to treat anxiety or agitated depression. Furthermore, it is slightly more effective than other TCAs or newer compounds. 7 , 8 Amitriptyline was initially used in 1961 where it replaced imipramine soon after. 9 Amitriptyline was the 3rd most frequently used antidepressant in Germany in 2008, corresponding to 94 million daily doses. 10 According to a large primary care-based prescription database in the UK, approximately 13 in every 1000 individuals were prescribed amitriptyline for depression treatment in 2010. 11 To date, it is one of the most commonly used antidepressants included in the WHO’s list of essential drugs. 12 Currently there are more than 20 types of antidepressants mentioned in the Chinese national essential drug list. However, only amitriptyline and doxepin are primarily prescribed by primary care physicians. 13 During amitriptyline metabolism, its side chain oxidizes producing a secondary amine nortriptyline, an N-oxide amitriptylinoxide (AT-NO), and a primary amine. 14 , 15 Also, the demethylation of amitriptyline to the secondary amine nortriptyline does not result in its inactivation. Therefore, nortriptyline, which also has antidepressant and antinociceptive activities, subsequently became available. 14 It is believed that the activities of amitriptyline and its active metabolite, nortriptyline, are primarily but not entirely due to their binding to the noradrenaline and serotonin transporters at central sites. 16 In addition to major depression, amitriptyline was also reported to treat chronic neuropathic pain (pain due to nerve damage), 17 , 18 fibromyalgia, 19 migraine, and anxiety disorders. 20 , 21 Although amitriptyline hydrochloride has been widely used in China for several years, only a limited number of reports have studied its efficacy and tolerability during treatment of depressive disorders or other diseases. Thus, the pharmacokinetic data of this drug are limited. Recently, a generic amitriptyline hydrochloride product has been developed by Hunan Dongting Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd., (Hunan, China). Consistent with National Medical Products Administration guidelines, we compared the bioavailability of the new amitriptyline hydrochloride tablets with the reference product, manufactured by Sandoz Inc. and listed in the FDA orange book in 2016. This study was performed in healthy Chinese subjects, under fasting and fed conditions, to support the marketing approval of the newly developed generic formulation in China. Materials and Methods Study Drugs The amitriptyline hydrochloride test product was obtained from Dongting Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd, Hunan, China (batch number XB170502, expiry date 2019/04). Meanwhile, the reference product was purchased from Sandoz Inc., US (batch number HB3649, expiry date 2020/04). Subjects Healthy male and female Chinese adults, aged 18 to 45 years, with body mass indexes (BMIs) ranging from 19 to 26 kg/m 2 , and weights higher than 45 and 55 kg for females and males, respectively, were recruited. All participating subjects signed informed consent forms (ICFs) after receiving information and confirmed understanding of the study’s nature, objectives, procedures, possible risks, and requirement for study completion. All subjects were subjected to a comprehensive medical examination to evaluate their health conditions, including routine physical examination, detailed medical history, routine clinical laboratory test (including analyses of the blood, coagulation function, urine, and immunological system, and drug, alcohol, and nicotine tests), 12-lead electrocardiography (12-lead ECG), and chest X-ray. Only healthy subjects, who agreed to use contraceptive methods from 14 days prior to dosing to 6 months following the end of study, and fit the age, BMI, and weight criteria, and signed the ICFs, fulfilled the inclusion criteria and thus were randomized. None of the subjects experienced any clinically significant abnormality during this study. Subjects with any history of allergy, sensitivity to any ingredient in the amitriptyline hydrochloride tablets, abuse of drug or alcohol, excessive smoking, or hepatic renal impairment were excluded. Subjects who used any drugs within 2 weeks before the first administration of amitriptyline hydrochloride, female subjects who were pregnant or lactating during the study, and subjects who suffered from any condition which could possibly affect the absorption of the drug were also excluded. Study Design and Treatment This study (ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03646526 ) was performed at the Phase I Clinical Research Center of the First Affiliated Hospital, College of Medicine, Zhejiang University, China, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, the Good Clinical Practice Guidelines of the International Conference on Harmonization, and other related guidelines. This study included two independent clinical trials (fasting and fed studies); each one was conducted using a randomized, open-label, single-dose, two-product, two-period crossover design. The research proposal was reviewed by the ethics committee of the First Affiliated Hospital, College of Medicine, Zhejiang University on February 8, 2018, and approved on March 20, 2018 (approval No. 2018-EC-38). The start and completion dates of the fasting and fed studies were August and September 2018, respectively. All the subjects who were hospitalized on the day before the trial were randomly assigned to either group TR or group RT. Group TR received the test product in the first treatment period and the reference product in the second treatment period, while Group RT had the opposite administration sequence. These two treatment periods were separated by a 3-week washout phase. The randomization scheme was generated by the SAS software (version 9.4) in a 1:1 randomized block design. For subjects under fasting conditions, a single-dose test or reference product was orally taken with 240 mL warm water after fasting for at least 10 h, while subjects under fed conditions had standard high-fat breakfast of about 800–1000 kcal (approximately 150, 250, and 500～600 kcal of protein, carbohydrates, and fat, respectively) starting 30 min before each drug administration and followed the same scheme. A thorough oral examination was performed after each drug administration to confirm oral film dissolution. The subjects were ambulatory, prohibited from vigorous activity, and closely supervised by qualified staff during the entire period of confinement. Water intake within 1 h before and after dosing was prohibited. Standard lunches and dinners were provided at the same time for both groups of the study, at 4 and 10 h after dosing. Blood Sampling and Analytical Determinations A series of blood samples were collected before and after each treatment period. Blood samples (4 mL) for pharmacokinetic analyses were collected into coded, K 2 -EDTA anticoagulation tubes at pre-dose (baseline) and at 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 24, 36, 48, 72, 96, 120, and 144 h post drug administration, and then centrifuged at 2000 × g and 4 °C for 10 min to separate the plasma. Plasma samples were temporarily stored at −20 °C within 2 h of collection and transferred to an ultra-low temperature freezer (−70 ± 10 °C) within 48 h for storage until analysis. In addition, all the collecting, processing, and storage procedures were performed under scarce light due to the photosensitive nature of the analytes. Plasma concentrations of amitriptyline and its metabolite nortriptyline were measured by the LC–MS/MS method, previously validated by CMIC (Suzhou) Pharmaceutical Technology Co., Ltd (Suzhou, China). After performing a protein precipitation procedure, the quantitative determination of the target compounds was carried out in the positive ion mode and multiple reaction monitoring. Analytes were chromatographed by Shimadzu LC-30AD and analyzed by AB SCIEX tandem mass spectrometry Triple Quad 5500. Data were acquired with the analyst software, version 1.6.3. The linearity range of the detection method for amitriptyline and nortriptyline were 0.2–50 ng/mL and 0.1～25 ng/mL, respectively. The lower limits of quantitation of amitriptyline and nortriptyline were 0.2 ng/mL and 0.1 ng/mL, respectively. Additionally, C max and AUC 0-t of amitriptyline were 18.7% and 14.9%, respectively. Based on previous pre-test results from 12 subjects, C max and AUC 0-t of amitriptyline were 23.48% and 18.95%, respectively. Thus, the coefficient of variation in this study was considered as 24%. Assuming a one-sided test with α = 0.05, accuracy of 0.8 (β = 0.2), CV intra-subject = 24%, a mean ratio of the test and reference product of 1.00, and 90% CI of 80.00%～125.00% for the bioequivalence, 21 samples were required for testing, according to the PASS software (version 11.0.7). After considering the dropout rate, 24 subjects were enrolled for each study. Safety Assessment Safety assessments included laboratory tests, physical examinations, 12-lead ECG, vital sign measurement, and incidence of AEs. The laboratory tests included analyses of blood, coagulation function, urine, and immunological examination. Meanwhile, vital signs, such as blood pressure, pulse, temperature, and respiratory rate, were monitored before administration, as well as at 1, 4, 6, 8, 24, 48, 72, 96, 120, 144 h after each drug administration to evaluate the safety of these two products. Any AEs occurring throughout the trial was recorded by research doctors and spontaneously reported by volunteers. Pharmacokinetic and Statistical Analysis Amitriptyline pharmacokinetic parameters were calculated using the statistical software package SAS Enterprise Guide (V9.4) (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, North Carolina) and verified by performing the non-compartmental analysis with the Phoenix WinNonlin software, version 7.0 (Certara, L.P., St. Louis, MO). Plasma concentration-time curves were generated under both fasting and fed conditions where C max and T max were obtained. Meanwhile, AUC 0−∞ was calculated using the linear trapezoidal rule. AUC 0–∞ was calculated as the sum of AUC 0−t and the extrapolated area from the last quantifiable concentration (Ct) divided by the elimination rate constant (λ z ). T 1/2 was calculated as ln2/λ z . The percentage of the extrapolated area (AUC _%Extrap_obs ) was obtained with the following formula: [(AUC 0−∞ -AUC 0−t )/AUC 0−∞ ] * 100%. The relative bioavailability (F) of the test product was calculated as: F=AUC 0-t (test)/AUC 0-t (reference) * 100%. Statistical analyses were performed with the statistical software package SAS Enterprise Guide (V9.4) (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, North Carolina) using the non-compartmental pharmacokinetic analysis. C max , AUC 0-t , and AUC 0-∞ were considered the main variables. The bioequivalence was determined by the factorial analysis of variance (ANOVA) for crossover design and calculating the 90% CIs of the ratio test/reference, according to the Chinese regulatory guideline. Therefore, ANOVA (PROC MIXED) evaluated the effects of the products, dosing sequence, trial period, and subjects nested within sequence by measuring the natural logarithm (ln)-transformed pharmacokinetic parameters (C max , AUC 0-t , and AUC 0-∞ ). Parametric 90% CIs of GMR between the two products (test–reference) were then calculated. Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test was used for T max and t 1/2 assessments. If the 90% CIs of the C max , AUC 0-t and AUC 0-∞ GMRs fell within 80% to 125%, the two products were considered bioequivalent. Safety Assessment During the study, all subjects received at least one dose of the study drug and were included in the safety analysis. During the fasting study, 83 AEs were recorded in all 24 subjects taking the test and reference products. The incidence of AEs of the test product was 100% (24/24), while that of the reference drug was 91.67% (22/24). All AEs were mild and reported as grade 1, except for one case of serum triglyceride increase after drug administration, which was reported as grade 2. In the fed study, 86 AEs were recorded in 24 subjects taking the test and reference products. The incidence of AEs of the test product was 95.83% (23/24); meanwhile, that of the reference was 100% (24/24). All AEs were mild and reported as grade 1, except for grade 3 sinus bradycardia in one case and grade 2 hypotension in another case. Drowsiness was the most frequently reported AE, and one of the most commonly described with the use of amitriptyline hydrochloride. 22 All AEs were spontaneously resolved without any specific treatment under fasting and fed conditions. The test and reference products were well tolerated and did not elicit serious adverse events (SAEs). In addition, no subject withdrew from the study due to AE ( Table 7 ). Both products were well tolerated, and no SAEs were reported. Bioequivalence was established considering the C max , AUC 0-t , and AUC 0-∞ of amitriptyline in both fasting and fed conditions. Statistical analysis of t 1/2 and T max for amitriptyline between the test and reference products under both fasting and fed conditions showed no significant difference when using the non-parametric method ( P > 0.05). However, the t 1/2 of nortriptyline was significant different between the test and reference products under fasting condition ( Table 8 ). In the fasting study, 5 subjects whose AUC _%Extrap_obs for nortriptyline exceeded 20% in both periods were excluded from the analysis, which may have contributed to the significance of t 1/2 . Amitriptyline undergoes demethylation forming the major metabolite nortriptyline. 14 Both amitriptyline and nortriptyline are active pharmaceutical ingredients and treat depression. 23 According to FDA’s Draft Guidance on Amitriptyline Hydrochloride, 24 the bioequivalence of the test and reference products is primarily determined by pharmacokinetic parameters (C max , AUC 0-t , and AUC 0-∞ ) of amitriptyline. The results of nortriptyline confirmed the bioequivalence between the generic and reference drugs. Under fasting and fed conditions, nortriptyline AUC _%Extrap_obs values were > 20% for 5 subjects in both periods and 3 patients in one or two periods, respectively, possibly due to insufficient blood collection time. Thus, a longer blood collection time may be necessary. In addition, subjects were not affected by the carryover effect since the amitriptyline and nortriptyline concentrations in the 2nd period were less than 5% C max , which proved enough washout time. The pharmacokinetic parameters of amitriptyline in this study were compared with those previously reported. 25 The observed C max for amitriptyline under fasting conditions was similar to previous reported, which validated our results. However, amitriptyline t 1/2 in this study was much longer than what is previously reported (24 h). Compared to previous reports, AUC 0-∞ increased by approximately 30% (296.87 ± 124.99 ng h/mL in the literature), while T max decreased by approximately 40% (the median value of 3.25 h in the literature). The pharmacokinetic difference between the parameters of this study and previous studies maybe influenced by different drugs’ manufacturers. 25 The amitriptyline hydrochloride used in literature is produced by Merck & Co, Inc., while the reference product in here was made by Sandoz Inc., US. Ethnicity difference could also be a reason, since previous studies were conducted using Korean subjects, while Chinese subjects were used in this study. In addition, the analytical determination methods may also play a role. Higher precision of the analytical instrument allows for detection of residual concentrations of chemicals, thus concentration-time curves closer to the actual pharmacokinetic characteristics can be obtained. Furthermore, pharmacokinetic data under fasting and fed conditions were compared. Tables 3 and 4 indicate that food had an impact on the pharmacokinetic processes of amitriptyline and nortriptyline, regardless of using the test or reference product. With the addition of standard high-fat breakfast before administration, C max of amitriptyline increased by approximately 20%. Lipophilic amitriptyline could have been absorbed with fat into the lacteals and therefore avoided the liver first-pass effect. In this case, the resulting higher plasma amitriptyline levels might have increased the amitriptyline C max . 26 Conversely, amitriptyline T max did not significantly change. Food inhibits the rate of gastric emptying, which increased the proportion of drugs dissolved prior to entering the small intestine thus delaying the rate of drug absorption. 27 The dissolution of lipophilic amitriptyline in bile salt micelles may promote drug absorption. Both the rate of gastric emptying and the lipophilicity of the drug may cause the invariance of T max . The amitriptyline t 1/2 , AUC 0−t , and AUC 0−∞ decreased; meanwhile, the nortriptyline T max was reduced by approximately 28%, and nortriptyline C max and AUC 0−t and AUC 0−∞ were increased by approximately 15%, 10%, and 10%, respectively. One possible explanation is that amitriptyline is preferably absorbed in the gastrointestinal tract and is metabolized in the liver. 28 Food can increase the hepatic-splanchnic blood flow, which may improve the metabolism of amitriptyline to nortriptyline. 29 This may account for the decreased t 1/2 , AUC 0−t , and AUC 0−∞ values of amitriptyline and the increased bioavailability of nortriptyline in the fed study, which confirms that food affected the pharmacokinetics of amitriptyline. Conclusion This study was conducted under both fasting and fed conditions, in healthy Chinese volunteers. Both the test and reference products complied with the regulatory criteria for supposing bioequivalence based on C max , AUC 0–t , and AUC 0-∞ . Title: Evaluation of model-based bioequivalence approach for single sample pharmacokinetic studies
Authors: Tardivon C, Loingeville F, Donnelly M, Feng K, Sun W, Sun G, Grosser S, Zhao L, Fang L, Mentré F, Bertrand J.
Citation: CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol. 2023 Jul;12(7):904-915. doi: 10.1002/psp4.12960. Epub 2023 Apr 27.
Abstract: In a traditional pharmacokinetic (PK) bioequivalence (BE) study, a two-way crossover study is conducted, PK parameters (namely the area under the time-concentration curve [AUC] and the maximal concentration [   C max    ]) are obtained by noncompartmental analysis (NCA), and the BE analysis is performed using the two one-sided test (TOST) method. For ophthalmic drugs, however, only one sample of aqueous humor, in one eye, per eye can be obtained in each patient, which precludes the traditional BE analysis. To circumvent this issue, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has proposed an approach coupling NCA with either parametric or nonparametric bootstrap (NCA bootstrap). The model-based TOST (MB-TOST) has previously been proposed and evaluated successfully for various settings of sparse PK BE studies. In this paper, we evaluate, via simulations, MB-TOST in the specific setting of single sample PK BE study and compare its performance to NCA bootstrap. We performed BE study simulations using a published PK model and parameter values and evaluated multiple scenarios, including study design (parallel or crossover), sampling times (5 or 10 spread across the dosing interval), and geometric mean ratio (of 0.8, 0.9, 1, and 1.25). Using the simulated structural PK model, MB-TOST performed similarly to NCA bootstrap for AUC. For   C max    , the latter tended to be conservative and less powerful. Our research suggests that MB-TOST may be considered as an alternative BE approach for single sample PK studies, provided that the PK model is correctly specified and the test drug has the same structural model as the reference drug.

Abstract In a traditional pharmacokinetic (PK) bioequivalence (BE) study, a two‐way crossover study is conducted, PK parameters (namely the area under the time‐concentration curve [AUC] and the maximal concentration [ C max ]) are obtained by noncompartmental analysis (NCA), and the BE analysis is performed using the two one‐sided test (TOST) method. For ophthalmic drugs, however, only one sample of aqueous humor, in one eye, per eye can be obtained in each patient, which precludes the traditional BE analysis. To circumvent this issue, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has proposed an approach coupling NCA with either parametric or nonparametric bootstrap (NCA bootstrap). The model‐based TOST (MB‐TOST) has previously been proposed and evaluated successfully for various settings of sparse PK BE studies. In this paper, we evaluate, via simulations, MB‐TOST in the specific setting of single sample PK BE study and compare its performance to NCA bootstrap. We performed BE study simulations using a published PK model and parameter values and evaluated multiple scenarios, including study design (parallel or crossover), sampling times (5 or 10 spread across the dosing interval), and geometric mean ratio (of 0.8, 0.9, 1, and 1.25). Using the simulated structural PK model, MB‐TOST performed similarly to NCA bootstrap for AUC. For C max , the latter tended to be conservative and less powerful.
